chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Emmett Berry: underrated trumpet and how Horace used him
summary: Berry came from Cleveland, played with Fletcher and Duke, used a Roy Eldridge-style mute, and Horace saved him for out choruses. He and Crosby were the core of the Omaha band.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: How about Emmett Berry? This was --

1940. Now that's a trumpet player that, in my estimation, that, unfortunately, he didn't get his just dues as a musician. What I mean by that, he didn't have anybody to actually push him. He played in Fletcher's band for quite a long time. We found him in Cleveland, Ohio, and he was another good reader, and he could punch, and he could play. And he always loved Roy Eldridge, and, you know, Roy had a mute called a mute, that little buzz music, sounded like a salt and pepper shaker on the end, you know, give it that -- Well, Emmett Berry got him one of those, and, boy, when he put that in there, he really sounded real good. And he could play. He could punch.
And he played a few things with Duke, and then he was with the name bands, but he would move around. He was one

of the guys that (inaudible) a few weeks back Roy and I discussed, and I asked him, "Do you hear from Emmett Berry?" He said, Horace, I haven't seen him for four or five years. He could be dead. I don't know. But during the era in the '40's that we were talking about he was a great trumpet player, and we thought that he had the makings of, you know, a great trumpet player -- and was going on, see. But somewhere along the road he wasn't pushed, and he didn't travel too much, and he didn't get his just dues but -- well, he was the type of trumpet player -- musically, I know the way I used him in my group, that I would save him for the outchorus, because he was strong, you know.

I'd let him play a solo, but I let him play it early in the arrangement. Then I'd even have him lay out, you know, a few bars just before the last chorus, and when we'd come out there, he'd pick the arrangement right up -- wouldn't miss a note, and he (inaudible). And he (inaudible), you know, you could see that he was dependable. And this is why I always liked him. And could play any part, first, second or third, he wasn't limited. We made a recording of "Chloe" that, one side John Kirby and his group made "Chloe" as the swing arrangement, and mine was more or less in the ballad form. And he did a chorus on "Chloe" that was a classic, him and Berry. John Hammond just idolized him. He really liked Emmett Berry. And, of course, and the great Israel Crosby, the Emmett Berry had a great ear (inaudible) music, that bassist who has recently passed -- they were great friends, (inaudible).

He was in my band, the band that I organized in Omaha, Nebraska. Israel Crosby were the only two Emmett Berry and (inaudible) fellows that I took there and built filled the rest of the band around these two guys.
I see. Yeah. I remember. We talked about that. In fact, the next person on the list is Israel Crosby.
